title: De insigni paradoxo, quod in analysi maximorum et minimorum occurrit

deep.reconstruction:
Context. Euler studies the variational problem of making J[y] = ∫ √x ds = ∫ √x √(1+p²) dx a minimum, where x is the depth below a horizontal line AB and p = dy/dx. On the previous page he obtained the first integral p√x/√(1+p²) = √a. Its extremals are the parabolas y = 2√(a(x−a)) (+ const). Each has its vertex E at depth a and its focus at depth 2a, so AB is their common directrix.

This page, §6 end. Along such a parabola ds = √x dx/√(x−a), so the integrand becomes x dx/√(x−a). Integrating from the vertex (x = a) to depth x: put u = x−a; then ∫(u+a)u^{-1/2} du = (2/3)u^{3/2} + 2a u^{1/2} = (2/3)(2a+x)√(x−a). By the theory this value 'ought' to be smaller than for any other curve joining E and Y.

§7. Euler builds a competitor, the broken path E→A→V→Y:
- EA goes straight up to the line x = 0 and costs ∫_0^a √x dx = (2/3)a^{3/2}.
- AV runs along the line x = 0, where the integrand vanishes, so it costs 0.
- VY goes straight down and costs (2/3)x^{3/2}.
The total is (2/3)(a^{3/2} + x^{3/2}). This exceeds the parabola value when x is not much larger than a, but is smaller when x is large. Example with a = 1, x = 100:
- parabola: (2/3)·102·√99 ≈ (2/3)·1015;
- broken path: (2/3)·1001.
So the extremal is not a minimum, which is the 'paradox' of the title.

Next page. He finds the crossover depth: (2a+x)√(x−a) = a√a + x√x, giving with a = 1 the cubic 3t³ − 2t² + 6t − 6 = 0 and x ≈ 221/121, i.e. just under 2.

Modern reading. The functional is Maupertuis/Jacobi action for a particle in uniform gravity: speed ∝ √(depth below the zero-energy line AB), and the extremals are projectile parabolas with directrix AB. Equivalently it is Fermat's principle with refractive index √x. Euler's competitor exploits the degenerate boundary x = 0, where the 'metric' x(dx² + dy²) vanishes. This is exactly the mechanism of the Goldschmidt discontinuous solution for the minimal surface of revolution (∫ y ds: catenary versus two disks joined along the axis). The phenomenon is that an extremal can be a local but not a global minimum, and the action is not least.
errors: Arithmetic approximation: √99 ≈ 9.94987, so 10 − 1/20 is better than Euler's 10 − 1/21 (= 9.9524). Either way 102·√99 ≈ 1014.9 ≈ 1015, so the conclusion is unaffected.

Logical gap (Euler's own point): the stationarity condition does not guarantee a minimum. The broken path is admissible only if 'curves' with vertical and horizontal segments, including ones along the degenerate line x = 0, are allowed. These are not smooth graphs y(x), which is exactly the issue later treated by Weierstrass/Goldschmidt-type analysis.
Euler's comparison 'multo major' is qualitative. The broken path already beats the parabola for x somewhat below 2a (crossover ≈ 1.82a), not only for 'much larger' x.

ideas.what: Evaluation of the functional along the extremal parabola: ∫ x dx/√(x−a) = (2/3)(2a+x)√(x−a)
ideas.modern_name: value function / action along an extremal

ideas.what: Counterexample: a broken path through the degenerate boundary x = 0 gives a smaller value than the extremal, so the extremal is not a (global) minimum
ideas.modern_name: failure of global minimality of an extremal; discontinuous (Goldschmidt-type) solution at a degenerate boundary; sufficiency problem
ideas.usually_credited_to: Goldschmidt (1831) for the minimal-surface analogue; Legendre (1786), Jacobi (1837), Weierstrass (1879) for sufficiency theory
ideas.where_published: E735 itself; unsure how fully it is discussed in Goldstine's or Fraser's histories

ideas.what: Extremals are parabolas with vertex depth equal to focal distance, i.e. common directrix AB
ideas.modern_name: projectile trajectories as action extremals (Maupertuis–Euler principle with v ∝ √depth)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1744 Methodus inveniendi, Additamentum II) for least action of projectiles

missed.claim: The functional ∫√x ds is precisely the Maupertuis/Euler action of a projectile with zero-energy level AB, so Euler's 'paradox' shows least action failing to be least for projectile motion. The mechanism is a degenerate-boundary (Goldschmidt-type) competitor, about 50 years before Goldschmidt's 1831 discontinuous solution for ∫ y ds. The page does not draw this link explicitly. Histories of 'action is not least' (e.g. Gray–Taylor) and of the Goldschmidt solution seldom cite E735 as a precursor, though I am unsure of the full literature.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a priority/attribution point: an early explicit example of an extremal beaten by a nonsmooth competitor using a degenerate boundary, in the very functional of Euler's own least-action principle.

deep.surprise_reason: Calculations are correct and elementary. The interest is historical: an explicit Goldschmidt-type counterexample showing an Euler–Lagrange extremal (and projectile least action) is not a minimum. E735 is a known paper, though perhaps under-credited.
